Description/Title: Harden TLS on hardware management controllers.
Discussion: Hardware management controllers (BMC, iLO, iDRAC, XCC, CIMC) provide privileged remote access below the operating system, so their web and API transports must not accept obsolete protocol versions or weak cryptographic profiles. Disable plaintext HTTP where the controller supports HTTPS-only operation; otherwise redirect HTTP to HTTPS without serving authenticated content over HTTP. Require TLS 1.2 or later (TLS 1.3 recommended) and disable weak protocol and cipher profiles. Evaluated via standard DMTF Redfish at /redfish/v1/Managers/{id}/NetworkProtocol (HTTP.ProtocolEnabled false or redirected, HTTPS.ProtocolEnabled true). Protects VCF SDDC Manager and VCF Operations out-of-band management workflows from credential interception.
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Older automation, browsers, monitoring systems, or centralized managers that support only obsolete TLS versions or cipher suites may stop connecting. Validate every management integration before enforcing the new profile. Disabling HTTP can also break discovery or redirects assumed by legacy tools; update those tools to use HTTPS directly.
Baseline Suggested Value: HTTPS only or HTTP permanently redirected to HTTPS; TLS 1.2 or later enforced; weak protocol and cipher profiles disabled

Description/Title: Use trusted certificates for hardware management controller communications.
Discussion: A hardware management controller's HTTPS identity certificate must be unique to that controller, within its validity period, match the management DNS name or address used by clients, and chain to a certificate authority trusted by administrators and management tools. Default factory self-signed certificates force automation to bypass certificate verification (e.g. ssl.CERT_NONE), exposing management traffic to adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Where LDAP or Active Directory authentication is enabled, the controller must also validate the directory server certificate against an approved trust anchor. Auditable via DMTF DSP2059 CertificateService (/redfish/v1/CertificateService/CertificateLocations or /redfish/v1/Managers/{id}/NetworkProtocol/HTTPS/Certificates).
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Replacing certificates or enabling directory certificate validation can interrupt management access when clients do not trust the issuing CA, names do not match, clocks are incorrect, or a directory server presents an incomplete chain. Stage approved trust anchors and test local break-glass access before enforcement.
Installation Default Value: Vendor self-signed HTTPS certificate; directory validation varies by vendor and configuration
Baseline Suggested Value: Unique valid CA-issued HTTPS certificate with matching identity; directory server certificate validation enabled whenever LDAP or Active Directory is used

Description/Title: Restrict SSH cryptography on hardware management controllers.
Discussion: SSH on a hardware management controller should remain disabled unless an operational workflow requires it, as required by esx-9.hardware-management-security. When SSH is retained, configure the controller's current approved cryptographic profile so that it excludes DSA host keys, SHA-1 key exchange, CBC ciphers, and other algorithms identified as weak. Evaluated via standard DMTF Redfish /redfish/v1/Managers/{id}/NetworkProtocol (SSH.ProtocolEnabled). If SSH is disabled, the control passes; if enabled, algorithms must adhere to current NIST SP 800-131Ar2 cryptographic transitions.
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Legacy SSH clients and automation that negotiate only removed algorithms may no longer connect. Confirm a supported management path and update clients before applying the profile. Do not weaken the controller profile solely to preserve an obsolete client; retain a documented break-glass path.
Baseline Suggested Value: SSH disabled unless required; when enabled, current approved cryptographic profile with weak key exchange, host-key, cipher, and MAC algorithms disabled

Description/Title: Harden integrated hardware management controllers and disable vulnerable legacy protocols.
Discussion: Servers with integrated hardware management controllers expose powerful features for monitoring, firmware updates, remote console, and out-of-band management. Reduce the attack surface by disabling unused protocols via DMTF Redfish /redfish/v1/Managers/{id}/NetworkProtocol: disable Telnet (Telnet.ProtocolEnabled false), disable IPMI-over-LAN (IPMI.ProtocolEnabled false) to eliminate cipher-0 authentication bypass and hash-exposure vulnerabilities (CVE-2013-4786), and disable SNMP (SNMP.ProtocolEnabled false) unless using SNMPv3 AuthPriv. Furthermore, enforce an idle session timeout <= 1800 seconds via /redfish/v1/SessionService (SessionTimeout <= 1800) to prevent unauthorized session reuse. Restrict physical and network access using dedicated management NICs and isolated VLANs. Transport-specific hardening is governed by esx-9.hardware-management-tls, esx-9.hardware-management-certificates, and esx-9.hardware-management-ssh-cryptography.
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Hardening controllers narrows the management surface, which can affect remote tools that previously relied on default open access or unauthenticated IPMI scripts. Most modern management tools support standard DMTF Redfish REST APIs. Disabling IPMI-over-LAN prevents legacy BMC polling; migrate monitoring to Redfish or vendor REST APIs.
Installation Default Value: Site-Specific (often IPMI-over-LAN and HTTP enabled by default)
Baseline Suggested Value: Unused controller services and protocols disabled, IPMI over LAN disabled, Telnet disabled, SNMPv1/v2c disabled, session timeout <= 1800s, vendor hardening guidance applied

Description/Title: Use strong, isolated identity management and brute-force protection on hardware management controllers.
Discussion: Hardware management controllers must be treated as Tier 0 administrative infrastructure. Their authentication should be isolated from managed workloads and general-purpose identity infrastructure to prevent circular recovery dependencies. Auditable via DMTF Redfish /redfish/v1/AccountService: enforce account lockout threshold between 1 and 5 failed attempts (AccountLockoutThreshold between 1 and 5) to block brute-force password guessing; require minimum password length >= 8 characters (MinPasswordLength >= 8, recommend >= 14); and where centralized directory authentication is used, verify ActiveDirectory.ServiceEnabled or LDAP.ServiceEnabled with dedicated management directory trees. Scripts and automation must authenticate using short-lived session tokens via /redfish/v1/SessionService rather than transmitting basic auth credentials with each request.
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Account lockout can result in denial of service if malicious or misconfigured systems repeatedly attempt failed logins with management usernames. Ensure a dedicated break-glass local administrator account exists with physical or serial console access.
Baseline Suggested Value: Strong authentication enabled, account lockout threshold between 1 and 5 failed attempts, min password length >= 8 (recommend >= 14), identity management isolated from managed systems

Description/Title: Synchronize hardware management controller time with organizational reference sources.
Discussion: Cryptography, audit logging, certificate validation, and incident response depend on consistent time across infrastructure. Hardware management controllers maintain independent real-time clocks and timestamp event logs (SEL); time drift from ESXi hosts and vCenter breaks log correlation and invalidates TLS certificates. Auditable via DMTF Redfish /redfish/v1/Managers/{id}/NetworkProtocol: verify NTP.ProtocolEnabled is true and NTP server addresses are configured with one reliable source or three or more sources (to avoid two-source split-brain condition). Where supported, configure authenticated NTP with symmetric keys to prevent time-tampering attacks.
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Synchronizing controller time to organizational NTP sources has no negative operational impact on workloads. Clocks with significant drift should be corrected during maintenance windows to avoid timestamp jumps in logs.
Installation Default Value: Site-Specific (often unconfigured or local RTC drift)
Baseline Suggested Value: Controller synchronized to organizational NTP sources, one source or three or more, NTP protocol enabled

Description/Title: Forward hardware management controller logs to a central log server over secure transport.
Discussion: Hardware management controllers maintain local non-volatile system event logs (SEL) recording logins, power state changes, firmware updates, hardware faults, and chassis intrusion events. Because local BMC logs have restricted storage capacities and can be wiped by an attacker, controllers must forward events to an organizational SIEM or VCF Log Management (formerly VMware Aria Operations for Logs). Where supported by the controller and destination, configure TLS transport with server certificate validation for remote syslog. Auditable via DMTF Redfish /redfish/v1/Managers/{id}/LogServices or NetworkProtocol syslog configurations.
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Forwarding logs requires network reachability from the BMC network to the syslog receiver and appropriate port/protocol configuration (e.g. TCP/TLS port 6514 or UDP port 514). Ensure firewall rules permit BMC outbound traffic to the log collector.
Baseline Suggested Value: Controller event logs forwarded to central log collector (VCF Log Management) using TLS transport where supported

Description/Title: Enable UEFI Secure Boot and verify out-of-band firmware attestation.
Discussion: UEFI Secure Boot uses cryptographic signatures to verify that every boot component (bootloader, ESX VMKernel, drivers, and signed VIBs) originated from a trusted vendor. Secure Boot is mandatory for modern VMware Cloud Foundation platforms: it is an explicit certification requirement in the VMware Compatibility Guide (VCG) for ESXi 8.0/9.0+ and serves as the cryptographic prerequisite for vSphere Trust Authority (vTA) and discrete TPM 2.0 Measured Boot (PCR 7). Without Secure Boot, hypervisor tamper-resistance cannot be established. In addition to in-band validation via PowerCLI, Secure Boot can be audited out-of-band via standard DMTF Redfish at /redfish/v1/Systems/{id}/SecureBoot (SecureBootEnable true, SecureBootCurrentBoot "Enabled").
Potential Functional Impact if Default V: Enabling Secure Boot causes ESX to refuse to load any boot component or kernel module that is not signed by an authorized key in the UEFI trust store. Before enabling on existing hosts, verify installed VIBs with the secureBoot.py verification utility. New VCF deployments inherit Secure Boot from standard commissioning images.
Installation Default Value: Site-Specific (often enabled on modern server shipments, but configurable)
Baseline Suggested Value: Enabled in system firmware and active for current boot
